title: Databases
description: Store and query data using relational and non-relational databases. Master SQL, indexing, transactions, NoSQL patterns, and data modeling.

topics.title: Relational Database Concepts
topics.content:
### Tables, Rows, and Relationships

A **relational database** organises data into **tables** (relations). Each table has:
- **Columns** (attributes): the fields defined in the schema.
- **Rows** (tuples): individual records.
- **Primary Key**: a column (or combination) that uniquely identifies each row.
- **Foreign Key**: a column that references a primary key in another table, creating a relationship.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email       VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  body        TEXT,
  author_id   INT REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);
```

#### Types of Relationships

| Relationship | Example | Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **One-to-Many** | One user → many posts | Foreign key on the "many" side |
| **Many-to-Many** | Users ↔ Roles | Junction table (`user_roles`) |
| **One-to-One** | User → Profile | Foreign key + UNIQUE constraint |

topics.title: SQL: Queries and Joins
topics.content:
### Writing Effective Queries

```sql
-- Basic SELECT
SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- Filtering and ordering
SELECT * FROM posts
WHERE author_id = 42 AND title ILIKE '%typescript%'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- Aggregations
SELECT
  author_id,
  COUNT(*)           AS post_count,
  MAX(created_at)    AS last_posted
FROM posts
GROUP BY author_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY post_count DESC;
```

#### Joins

```sql
-- INNER JOIN: only matching rows from both tables
SELECT p.title, u.name AS author
FROM posts p
INNER JOIN users u ON p.author_id = u.id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all posts, even those with no matching user
SELECT p.title, u.name AS author
FROM posts p
LEFT JOIN users u ON p.author_id = u.id;

-- Multiple joins
SELECT p.title, u.name, COUNT(c.id) AS comment_count
FROM posts p
JOIN users u ON p.author_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN comments c ON c.post_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, u.name
ORDER BY comment_count DESC;
```

topics.title: Indexing and Query Optimization
topics.content:
### Why Queries Get Slow

Without an index, a query does a **full table scan** — reading every row. On a table with 10 million rows, this is catastrophic.

An index is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations.

```sql
-- Slow: full table scan on 10M row table
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';

-- Add an index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Now: index lookup → O(log n) instead of O(n)

-- Composite index: covers queries filtering by both columns
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_author_created ON posts(author_id, created_at DESC);

-- Unique index (also enforces uniqueness)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);

-- Partial index: only indexes rows matching a condition
CREATE INDEX idx_users_active ON users(created_at) WHERE active = true;
```

#### EXPLAIN ANALYZE

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM posts WHERE author_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC;

-- Look for:
-- Seq Scan  → no index used (slow on large tables)
-- Index Scan → index used (fast)
-- Rows Removed by Filter → index not selective enough
```

#### When NOT to Index
- Tables with < 10,000 rows (full scans are fast)
- Columns with low cardinality (e.g., a boolean column)
- Columns that are written very frequently (indexes slow writes)

topics.title: Transactions and ACID
topics.content:
### Making Multiple Operations Atomic

A **transaction** groups multiple SQL statements so they either all succeed or all fail.

```sql
-- Transfer $100 from Alice to Bob
BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE user_id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE user_id = 2;

-- Only commits if BOTH updates succeed
COMMIT;

-- Or roll back everything on failure
ROLLBACK;
```

#### ACID Properties

| Property | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Atomicity** | All-or-nothing: either every statement commits or none do. |
| **Consistency** | A transaction takes the DB from one valid state to another. |
| **Isolation** | Concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial changes. |
| **Durability** | Committed data survives crashes (written to disk). |

#### Isolation Levels

```sql
-- Default (Read Committed): sees only committed data
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

-- Repeatable Read: sees same data for duration of transaction
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

-- Serializable: strictest — transactions run as if sequential
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
```
